name: Darwin Gödel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents
authors: Jenny Zhang, Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Robert Lange, Jeff Clune (co-first: Zhang & Hu; co-senior: Lange & Clune); lead affiliations: University of British Columbia / Vector Institute / Sakana AI / Canada CIFAR AI Chair
venue: Accepted as ICLR 2026 Poster (OpenReview id pUpzQZTvGY); first released as arXiv preprint (arXiv:2505.22954, submitted 29 May 2025, latest v3 12 Mar 2026)
reflection_type: search-guided | tool-verified — population/evolutionary open-ended search over self-generated code modifications, where each candidate is empirically validated on coding benchmarks; agents also analyze their own benchmark evaluation logs to propose the next self-improvement (a form of log-based self-diagnosis), and discovered workflow improvements include using another FM as a peer-reviewer/judge to select among multiple attempts
feedback_source: external-tool / benchmark evaluation: each self-modified agent is empirically validated on coding benchmark subsets (SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot), with success measured by passing the tasks' tests; a foundation model proposes the modification from the agent's own evaluation logs (self-generated proposal grounded in empirical benchmark scores). No ground-truth test results are revealed to the agent during evaluation (pass@1 setting on Polyglot).
iteration_structure: population/evolutionary — open-ended archive-based search (Darwinian). Starting from one base agent, 80 iterations generate one new agent per iteration; parents are sampled from a growing archive (selection roughly proportional to performance score and inversely to number of children), self-modify, are evaluated, and surviving agents (compile + retain codebase-editing ability) are added back to the archive, forming a branching tree of agents (parallel exploration of many lineages).
reflection_object: agent's own code/architecture — the DGM reflects on and rewrites its own Python codebase (the coding agent's tools, prompts, and workflows, e.g., finer-grained edit tools, long-context/history summarization, multiple solution attempts with FM-based peer-review selection). Self-improvement is framed as a coding task that modifies the agent's own components. The underlying foundation-model weights are NOT modified (frozen FMs), and the open-ended exploration / archive-maintenance process itself is fixed and not modifiable.
learning_locus: in_context_verbal (no weight update) — despite the item metadata labeling it gradient_weight_update, the actual mechanism modifies the agent's source code (prompts, tools, workflows) on top of FROZEN pretrained foundation models; no gradient/weight updates are performed in this version. The paper explicitly lists rewriting its own training script to update the FM weights as future work, not implemented here.
requires_training: none — no SFT/RL/DPO; foundation models are frozen. Improvement comes from evolutionary search over self-written code, not from parameter updates.
reward_or_critic_model: verifiable reward (empirical benchmark pass-rate on coding tasks) drives parent selection/survival; additionally a discovered workflow uses a separate FM as a self-judge/peer-reviewer to pick the best among multiple solution attempts (self-as-judge at the task-solving level). No trained reward model.
distillation_target: reusable-skill/workflow + agent code — improvements are distilled into the agent's own code repository (better edit tools, context-window management, multi-attempt + peer-review workflow), persisted as archived agents (a population of code artifacts). Not distilled into model weights.
emergent_vs_engineered: engineered scaffold/search with emergent discoveries — the open-ended evolutionary scaffold, archive, and parent-selection are human-designed and fixed, but the specific tool/workflow innovations (granular editing, history summarization, peer-review selection, considering prior attempts) are autonomously discovered/emergent within that search, not hand-coded by the authors.
memory_type: skill-library / archive — a growing Darwinian archive (tree) of all discovered coding agents serves as the long-term store of reusable code-based skills/workflows; each agent also has short-term scratchpad context and discovered long-context history summarization within a task.
memory_persistence: cross-task / cross-iteration — the archive persists across all 80 iterations of a run; archived agents act as stepping stones that can be branched from much later than their discovery. Discovered improvements also transfer cross-benchmark and cross-model (held-out evaluations).
memory_curation_mechanism: population-or-Pareto-selected (archive growth gated by validity) — every newly generated agent that compiles AND retains codebase-editing functionality is added to the archive (append to population); agents that lose editing ability or fail to compile are discarded. The archive itself is append-only over a run; parent selection (score-proportional, child-count-inverse) curates which lineages get explored rather than pruning the archive.
error_localization_granularity: agent-level / block-level (code) — modifications target whole functional components of the agent's codebase (specific tools, workflow blocks); the agent diagnoses weaknesses from its own evaluation logs and proposes a single next feature/fix, operating at the level of code blocks/components rather than token-level or single-response level.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: inter-task (cross-generation) — the core learning is transferring improvements across iterations/generations of agents and across tasks/benchmarks (self-improvement of the agent design), not refining a single task answer. (A discovered intra-task workflow does make multiple attempts within one task and picks the best.)
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: avoidance / escape via open-ended search — failed or degraded self-modifications are discarded (avoidance); because branching can occur from any archived agent with non-zero probability, the DGM can escape deceptive performance dips (e.g., recovered after dips at iterations 4 and 56 on SWE-bench) by branching from earlier stepping-stones rather than only from the latest best.
task_domains: code (software engineering / automated program repair + multi-language coding); the method is a self-improving coding agent. Preliminary safety-oriented extension explores FM hallucination countermeasures (Appendix H).
benchmarks: SWE-bench (SWE-bench Verified subset; also SWE-bench-verified-mini for staged eval) and Polyglot (Aider Polyglot, multi-language: C++, Rust, Python, etc.)
headline_result: On SWE-bench Verified, the DGM autonomously improved the coding agent from 20.0% to 50.0% over 80 iterations; on the full Polyglot benchmark it improved from 14.2% to 30.7% (38.0% on the 50-task Polyglot eval subset). Base/best agents both use frozen FMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) for SWE-bench self-mod and eval; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) self-mod + o3-mini eval for Polyglot).
baselines: Two ablation baselines: 'DGM w/o self-improve' (fixed base meta-agent, replicating ADAS in this setting) and 'DGM w/o open-ended exploration' (no archive; always self-modifies the latest valid version). Also compared to handcrafted open-source agents: checked SoTA open-source SWE-bench solution, and Aider (representative Polyglot agent).
gains_vs_baseline: DGM outperforms both ablation baselines on SWE-bench and Polyglot: removing self-improvement causes gains to taper off quickly after early iterations; removing open-ended exploration makes recovery from poor self-modifications hard. Final DGM agent (+30.0 pts on SWE-bench, 20.0%->50.0%) is comparable to the checked human-designed open-source SoTA on SWE-bench, and on Polyglot the discovered agent far surpasses Aider. Transfer: best SWE-bench agent reaches 28.9% on held-out Polyglot (vs 14.2% base); best Polyglot agent reaches 24.5% on held-out SWE-bench (vs 20.0% base). Model transfer: with o3-mini, base 23.0% -> DGM 33.0%; with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, base 19.0% -> DGM 59.5% (SWE-bench, 200 tasks).
compute_cost_profile: Very high training/search cost: a single DGM run on SWE-bench takes ~2 weeks and ~USD 22,000 in API costs (vs ~USD 10,000 for either ablation baseline). 80 iterations with staged evaluation (10 -> 50/60 -> 200 tasks). Per-evaluation cost estimates: ~USD 350 for 60 SWE-bench tasks (Claude 3.5 Sonnet New); ~USD 5 for 60 Polyglot tasks (o3-mini). Higher-performing discovered agents also incur greater inference cost than the base agent, though cost and performance are not strictly correlated.
known_limitations: Requires extensive compute (~2 weeks, ~$22k per SWE-bench run); still falls short of closed-source SoTA SWE-bench solutions. Inherently bounded by the frozen FM's capabilities (esp. reasoning); does not yet modify FM weights. The open-ended exploration/archive process is itself fixed and not self-modifiable. Assumes coding-benchmark performance is a good proxy for self-improvement ability (alignment that may not hold beyond coding). Safety risks: optimizing solely for a benchmark could amplify misalignment over generations and produce increasingly uninterpretable code; mitigated via sandboxing, time limits, traceable archive lineage, and human oversight. Single-objective tie of self-improvement to one benchmark (co-evolving tasks left as future work).
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: external-tool/verifier (benchmark test execution) — improvement signal comes from empirical pass-rates on coding benchmark tests, i.e., verifiable execution-grounded feedback. Notably, on Polyglot it uses pass@1 where the agent NEVER sees ground-truth test results (unlike the leaderboard's pass@2), so it is not oracle-label leakage; survival/selection depends on this external test-based evaluation rather than intrinsic self-verification alone.
self_correction_efficacy: net-positive (in the coding-self-improvement domain) — sustained performance gains across iterations on both benchmarks; ablations show that BOTH self-improvement and open-ended exploration are required for continued gains (removing either causes stagnation or brittle recovery). Gains generalize across models, benchmarks, and languages (held-out tests), indicating real skill acquisition rather than benchmark overfitting. Efficacy is contingent on a meaningful empirical evaluation signal.
calibration_effect: not-measured — the paper does not report a confidence-calibration analysis; its 'reflection' is at the agent-design/search level, not reasoning-confidence calibration.
failure_attribution_capability: classifies/diagnoses-from-logs (lightweight) — each agent analyzes its own benchmark evaluation logs to identify weaknesses and propose the next improvement, a form of self-diagnosis of failing behavior; however the paper does not present a formal failure-mode taxonomy or per-step counterfactual attribution. Not a dedicated failure-attribution method.
failure_mode_addressed: Targets and self-fixes coding-agent capability gaps: imprecise/coarse file editing (improved to line-level viewing and string-replacement editing), context-window overflow on long trajectories (added history summarization / long-context management), and single-shot brittleness (added multiple attempts plus FM peer-review selection and consideration of prior attempts). Broadly addresses stagnation/local-optima in agent self-design via open-ended archive search. Not mapped to MAST's multi-agent failure taxonomy.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new benchmark released; uses existing SWE-bench Verified (and SWE-bench-verified-mini) and Aider Polyglot. The DGM system code and discovered agent archive are open-sourced at https://github.com/jennyzzt/dgm.
builds_on: Gödel machine (Schmidhuber, 2007/1987); Darwinian evolution & open-endedness / quality-diversity research (Stanley & Lehman; Clune 2019 AI-Generating Algorithms; Zhang et al. 2024 OMNI-EPIC; Faldor et al. 2025); ADAS — Automated Design of Agentic Systems (Hu et al., 2025, the 'DGM w/o self-improve' baseline); Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2024) and STOP / Self-Taught Optimizer (Zelikman et al., 2024) self-modifying scaffolds; FM tool-use agents (Schick et al. 2023 Toolformer; Anthropic Claude). Benchmarks: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), Polyglot/Aider (Gauthier, 2024).
extended_by_or_inspired: HyperAgents / DGM-Hyperagents (DGM-H, arXiv:2603.19461) — extends DGM to make the meta-level self-modification procedure itself editable and generalizes beyond coding (paper review, robotics reward design, Olympiad-math grading); Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM, arXiv:2510.21614, OpenReview T0EiEuhOOL) — guides self-modification by an estimated Clade Metaproductivity (CMP) and outperforms DGM and SICA on SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot; Self-Improving Coding Agent (SICA, Robeyns et al., 2025); POLARIS Gödel-agent framework for small LMs (arXiv:2603.23129); GODEGEN / 'The Living Agent' production evolutionary self-improvement.
reasoning_model_native: Partially / model-agnostic — the DGM uses frozen FMs and is not specific to reasoning models, but it was run with and transfers across both standard and reasoning-style models (Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, OpenAI o3-mini used for Polyglot eval and SWE-bench transfer). Its reflection is at the code/scaffold level, not reliant on a model's built-in reflection.
on_policy_distillation_link: Indirect — the DGM distills self-discovered improvements into reusable code/workflows (a skill-library/scaffold-optimization analogue) rather than into weights; it is related to skill/workflow optimization and agent self-design, but does not perform on-policy distillation into model parameters (FMs are frozen). Updating the FM via self-rewritten training scripts is named as future work.
sample_efficiency: Low / compute-heavy: ~80 search iterations (one new agent per iteration) over ~2 weeks and ~USD 22,000 to raise SWE-bench from 20.0% to 50.0%; staged evaluation (10 -> 50/60 -> up to 200 tasks per agent) is used to limit cost. The authors explicitly cite low efficiency as a limitation and call for more compute-efficient variants.
